Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

The use of generative AI is declared at the end of the main text, under "Declaration of generative AI use".
Does narcissistic personality disorder involve expressive language disorder?
The question sounds clinical, yet a direct search finds nothing to review.
In November 2026, a PubMed search of titles and abstracts that paired narcissism with "expressive language," "language disorder," or "language impairment" returned no records.
The empty result points to a mismatch of levels between the two concepts.
Expressive language disorder is a developmental category of structural language that concerns vocabulary, grammar, and sentence production (World Health Organization [WHO], 1992, F80.1).
Current systems place it under language disorder (American Psychiatric Association [APA], 2022), and an international consensus uses the term developmental language disorder (Bishop et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Current systems place it under language disorder (American Psychiatric Association [APA], 2022), and an international consensus uses the term developmental language disorder <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bishop et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: The current manual also lists social (pragmatic) communication disorder, introduced with DSM-5 for difficulty in the social use of communication (APA, 2022; Norbury, 2014).
text.formatted: The current manual also lists social (pragmatic) communication disorder, introduced with DSM-5 for difficulty in the social use of communication <ref type="bibr">(APA, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Norbury, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: That category does not fit either, as Section 3.1 shows.
Nothing in the diagnostic description of narcissistic personality disorder involves missing vocabulary or grammar (APA, 2022).
text.formatted: Nothing in the diagnostic description of narcissistic personality disorder involves missing vocabulary or grammar <ref type="bibr">(APA, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: In a population sample of 9-year-olds, narcissistic traits even went with higher verbal ability (Fontaine et al., 2008).
text.formatted: In a population sample of 9-year-olds, narcissistic traits even went with higher verbal ability <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Fontaine et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: The difficulties lie elsewhere: in putting feelings into words, and in negotiating meaning with another person.
The evidence that does exist looks contradictory.
A recent meta-analysis of 14 studies (N = 8,006) found that narcissism as a whole is unrelated to alexithymia (r = .03; Song et al., 2026).
text.formatted: A recent meta-analysis of 14 studies (N = 8,006) found that narcissism as a whole is unrelated to alexithymia (r = .03; <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Song et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Beneath that null lie opposite signs.
In the same meta-analysis, grandiose narcissism correlated negatively with alexithymia (r = -.08), whereas samples that combined vulnerable and grandiose measures correlated positively (r = .09).
Vulnerable narcissism was measured in just one of the included studies.
Communication research shows a second split.
Speakers high in narcissism expect to persuade in speech and in writing, but raters credit their speeches and discount their essays (Foster et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Speakers high in narcissism expect to persuade in speech and in writing, but raters credit their speeches and discount their essays <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Foster et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Even the most intuitive linguistic marker fails, because narcissism is unrelated to the use of first-person singular pronouns (Carey et al., 2015).
text.formatted: Even the most intuitive linguistic marker fails, because narcissism is unrelated to the use of first-person singular pronouns <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Carey et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: These splits carry concrete costs.
First, assessment relies on self-report, and the grandiose pole reports more skill than it shows.
Narcissism correlates positively with self-reported emotional intelligence and negatively with ability measures of it (Michels & Schulze, 2021).
text.formatted: Narcissism correlates positively with self-reported emotional intelligence and negatively with ability measures of it <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Michels & Schulze, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: People high in grandiose narcissism also rate their empathy more highly than people high in vulnerable narcissism, while objective measures are rarely given alongside (Eddy, 2021).
text.formatted: People high in grandiose narcissism also rate their empathy more highly than people high in vulnerable narcissism, while objective measures are rarely given alongside <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Eddy, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: A self-report alexithymia score can therefore classify a fluent but affectively thin speaker as emotionally skilled.
Second, the vulnerable pole, where an expressive deficit is most plausible, is almost unmeasured.
Third, the two poles call for different help.
A person who cannot name a feeling needs support in naming it.
A person who speaks well but cannot let speech change in dialogue needs something else.
Pooling the poles under one construct hides both needs from the clinicians who assess them.
This review therefore changes the question.
It asks whether narcissism involves a domainspecific failure at the interface of affect and pragmatic form.
It also asks whether that failure takes different shapes at the grandiose and vulnerable poles.
To answer it, the review uses Weber's ideal-type method as Etzrodt (2022) extends it.
text.formatted: To answer it, the review uses Weber's ideal-type method as <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Etzrodt (2022)</ref> extends it.

text.text: Concepts are defined clearly, their consequences are derived consistently, and each derived claim is exposed to refutation.
The review also borrows a conceptual pair from Etzrodt's (2024) reading of Weber, which treats Durkheimian anomie and Marxist alienation as opposites.
text.formatted: The review also borrows a conceptual pair from <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Etzrodt's (2024)</ref> reading of Weber, which treats Durkheimian anomie and Marxist alienation as opposites.

text.text: Anomie is "formless life," and alienation is "lifeless form" (Thom, 1984 , as cited in Etzrodt, 2024, p. 660).
text.formatted: Anomie is "formless life," and alienation is "lifeless form" <ref type="bibr">(Thom, 1984</ref> <ref type="bibr">, as cited in Etzrodt, 2024, p. 660)</ref>.

text.text: Transposed to expression, the pair names two opposite failures of one relation.
Affect finds no form, or a form keeps out the affect that would change it.
The review makes six contributions.
First, it relocates the expressive difficulty from structural language to the relation between affect and form, which explains why direct searches find nothing.
Second, it reads the near-zero meta-analytic correlation as the sum of two opposite failures rather than as the absence of one.
Third, it explains why grandiose self-reports diverge from performance: the divergence is a predicted property of one ideal type.
Fourth, it identifies shame as the affect on which both poles fail, in opposite ways.
Unlike a general alexithymia account, it therefore predicts that naming failures concentrate on shame and related selfconscious emotions.
Fifth, it explains why developmental language disorder raises the risk of personality disorder without a dose-response relation to language severity.
Sixth, it states seven propositions, each with the observation that would refute it, and shows where they separate the types from three rival accounts.
Weber constructed ideal types by accentuating selected features of a phenomenon into a consistent conceptual picture that no concrete case matches exactly (Weber, 1949).
text.formatted: Weber constructed ideal types by accentuating selected features of a phenomenon into a consistent conceptual picture that no concrete case matches exactly <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Weber, 1949)</ref>.

text.text: Because concept formation follows the researcher's interests, objectivity (better called intersubjectivity) rests on clear definitions applied systematically (Etzrodt, 2024, p. 667). Etzrodt (2022) argues that this consistency is necessary but not sufficient, since a consistently derived interpretation can still be false.
text.formatted: Because concept formation follows the researcher's interests, objectivity (better called intersubjectivity) rests on clear definitions applied systematically <ref type="bibr">(Etzrodt, 2024, p. 667)</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Etzrodt (2022)</ref> argues that this consistency is necessary but not sufficient, since a consistently derived interpretation can still be false.

text.text: Popper's falsificationism supplies the missing step: general statements cannot be verified, but they can fail against observation (Popper, 1959). Etzrodt (2022) adds a condition from Schutz.
text.formatted: Popper's falsificationism supplies the missing step: general statements cannot be verified, but they can fail against observation <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Popper, 1959)</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Etzrodt (2022)</ref> adds a condition from Schutz.

text.text: The researcher's interpretation of actors' motives must itself be tested in concrete situations.
The method suits narcissism for a specific reason.
Grandiose and vulnerable narcissism are not separate kinds of people.
Clinical reviewers treat grandiosity and vulnerability as two phenotypic themes (Pincus & Lukowitsky, 2010).
text.formatted: Clinical reviewers treat grandiosity and vulnerability as two phenotypic themes <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Pincus & Lukowitsky, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: They warn that labels such as overt and covert narcissism wrongly turn these two modes of expression into separate types.
Structural work finds dimensions, and its most parsimonious solution has three factors: agentic extraversion, narcissistic neuroticism, and self-centered antagonism (Crowe et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Structural work finds dimensions, and its most parsimonious solution has three factors: agentic extraversion, narcissistic neuroticism, and self-centered antagonism <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Crowe et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Momentary data show movement between the themes, because people who are dispositionally grandiose report vulnerable as well as grandiose states over time (Edershile & Wright, 2021).
text.formatted: Momentary data show movement between the themes, because people who are dispositionally grandiose report vulnerable as well as grandiose states over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Edershile & Wright, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: If the two forms are treated as subtypes, these facts are anomalies.
If they are treated as ideal-typical poles, the facts are expected, because a person can stand at different distances from each pole and move between them.
The review proceeds in four steps.
It defines the relation between affect and form and its two failures.
It derives each ideal type and sets it against the evidence.
It places developmental language disorder relative to the types.
Finally, it states each derived claim as a proposition with a refutation condition.
The evidence was located through searches of PubMed, OpenAlex, and the Semantic Scholar corpus in November 2026.
Meta-analyses and systematic reviews were preferred wherever they exist, and primary studies were used where no synthesis is available.
Sources published online first are cited by their issue year.
The evidence comes from four literatures that seldom cite one another, and the next section sorts them by what each leaves unresolved.
>Four literatures and what each leaves unresolved
text.formatted: <head n="3." >Four literatures and what each leaves unresolved</head>

text.text: Developmental language research defines language difficulty structurally, and its outcome studies treat childhood language disorder as a risk marker.
In an Ottawa cohort followed from age 5, children with early language impairment had more anxiety disorders at age 19, mostly social phobia (Beitchman et al., 2001).
text.formatted: In an Ottawa cohort followed from age 5, children with early language impairment had more anxiety disorders at age 19, mostly social phobia <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Beitchman et al., 2001)</ref>.

text.text: The same study found higher rates of antisocial personality disorder among boys with language impairment.
In a Danish clinical cohort, 469 people diagnosed with developmental language disorder in childhood were compared with 2,345 matched controls (Mouridsen & Hauschild, 2009).
text.formatted: In a Danish clinical cohort, 469 people diagnosed with developmental language disorder in childhood were compared with 2,345 matched controls <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Mouridsen & Hauschild, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Over a mean follow-up of 34.7 years, a personality disorder diagnosis was registered for 4.9% of the cases and 2.2% of the controls (Mouridsen & Hauschild, 2009).
text.formatted: Over a mean follow-up of 34.7 years, a personality disorder diagnosis was registered for 4.9% of the cases and 2.2% of the controls <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Mouridsen & Hauschild, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: This literature leaves two questions open.
It cannot isolate narcissism, because registry diagnoses follow the ICD, which has no separate category for narcissistic personality disorder.
ICD-10 lists it under other specific personality disorders (WHO, 1992, F60.8).
It also shows risk without explaining it, because the severity of childhood expressive and receptive impairment did not predict a later diagnosis (Mouridsen & Hauschild, 2009).
text.formatted: It also shows risk without explaining it, because the severity of childhood expressive and receptive impairment did not predict a later diagnosis <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Mouridsen & Hauschild, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: The nearest diagnostic neighbor is social (pragmatic) communication disorder, which describes persistent difficulty with the social use of verbal and nonverbal communication (Norbury, 2014).
text.formatted: The nearest diagnostic neighbor is social (pragmatic) communication disorder, which describes persistent difficulty with the social use of verbal and nonverbal communication <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Norbury, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: It too misses the narcissistic case.
It is a developmental profile that appears across neurodevelopmental disorders, and its pragmatic difficulties depend in part on structural language (Norbury, 2014).
text.formatted: It is a developmental profile that appears across neurodevelopmental disorders, and its pragmatic difficulties depend in part on structural language <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Norbury, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: The difficulties linked to narcissism instead vary with threats to the self and change under instruction (Hepper et al., 2014; Janusz et al., 2021).
text.formatted: The difficulties linked to narcissism instead vary with threats to the self and change under instruction <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Hepper et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Janusz et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Developmental language research therefore offers no category, structural or pragmatic, for a failure that depends on affect.
Personality research shows that the emotional correlates of narcissism split by pole.
The alexithymia split described above is one example (Song et al., 2026).

text.text: This literature leaves the expressive question open.
Most of it rests on self-report, which the grandiose pole inflates (Michels & Schulze, 2021).

text.text: It also describes emotional dispositions without saying how affect becomes speech that another person can take up.
Language-use research asks what people high in narcissism actually say.
The folk marker failed.
Across five laboratories and 4,811 participants, narcissism was unrelated to the use of firstperson singular pronouns (Carey et al., 2015).

text.text: It correlated negatively with anxiety words, tentative words, and perceptual words, and every effect was smaller than |r| = .10.
Persuasion studies reveal a gap between claimed and credited skill.
People high in narcissism rate their creativity more highly than blind coders do, yet they persuade targets when pitching ideas, partly through enthusiasm (Goncalo et al., 2010).

text.text: This literature leaves the mechanism open.
It records markers and outcomes but offers no account of why fluency should help in one modality and fail in another.
Its modality contrast also comes from separate studies whose samples and methods differ, so its authors caution against comparing the modalities directly (Foster et al., 2025).

text.text: Interaction research follows narcissism across meetings and turns of talk.
At zero acquaintance, people high in narcissism are more popular, and the entitled and exploitative aspects of narcissism are the most attractive at first sight (Back et al., 2010).
text.formatted: At zero acquaintance, people high in narcissism are more popular, and the entitled and exploitative aspects of narcissism are the most attractive at first sight <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Back et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Over repeated meetings the picture reverses.
In discussion groups that met seven times, self-enhancers made positive first impressions and were rated negatively by the seventh week (Paulhus, 1998).
text.formatted: In discussion groups that met seven times, self-enhancers made positive first impressions and were rated negatively by the seventh week <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Paulhus, 1998)</ref>.

text.text: In a three-week group study, narcissistic admiration had an initially positive but declining effect on popularity (Leckelt et al., 2015).

text.text: Narcissistic rivalry had a growing negative effect, carried by arrogant and aggressive behavior.
Repair, in the relational sense used here, means acknowledging, apologizing for, or revising one's own contribution.
It is the clearest casualty.
Narcissism predicts unwillingness to apologize through low empathy and low guilt, and the effect belongs to rivalry rather than admiration (Leunissen et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Narcissism predicts unwillingness to apologize through low empathy and low guilt, and the effect belongs to rivalry rather than admiration <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Leunissen et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Conversation analysis of couple therapy shows clients with narcissistic problems resisting questions, controlling the topic, and displaying independence (Janusz et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Conversation analysis of couple therapy shows clients with narcissistic problems resisting questions, controlling the topic, and displaying independence <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Janusz et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: These moves appeared when the first consultation threatened their self-image.
This literature describes conduct but not the expressive process behind it.
It shows that collaboration fails over time without saying what fails in the speaker's expression.
The four literatures meet at one relation that none of them measures directly.
The question is whether a speaker's affect reaches a linguistic form that a listener can take up, and whether that form stays open to revision in dialogue.
Developmental research measures form without affect, and personality research measures affect without form.
Language-use research counts forms without their affective source, and interaction research records outcomes without their expressive mechanism.
This review takes the relation itself as its object and argues that narcissism disturbs it in two opposite ways.
Expression, in the sense used here, is the act of giving affect a linguistic form that another person can take up.
The form is pragmatic because it is addressed to a listener.
It is judged by what it offers for uptake and by whether it can change in the exchange.
Expression succeeds under two conditions.
The form must carry the affect, which means that the feeling is identified and named.
The form must also stay open, which means that the speaker can revise or withdraw it in response to the listener.

Conversation analysis finds this openness in ordinary talk: speakers routinely repair trouble in their own utterances, and self-correction is preferred to correction by others (Schegloff et al., 1977).
text.formatted: Conversation analysis finds this openness in ordinary talk: speakers routinely repair trouble in their own utterances, and self-correction is preferred to correction by others <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Schegloff et al., 1977</ref>).

text.text: Weber's typology of action clarifies the first condition.

In Etzrodt's (2024, p. 661) summary, Weber derived four ideal types of action: traditional action based on habituation, affectual action based on emotion, value-rational action, and purposive-rational action.
text.formatted: In <ref type="bibr">Etzrodt's (2024, p. 661)</ref> summary, Weber derived four ideal types of action: traditional action based on habituation, affectual action based on emotion, value-rational action, and purposive-rational action.

text.text: Weber placed purely affectual behavior at the borderline of meaningful action and often beyond it, as in an uncontrolled reaction to an exceptional stimulus.
Affect enters the field of meaning when it is released consciously, which Weber called sublimation (Weber, 1978, p. 25).
text.formatted: Affect enters the field of meaning when it is released consciously, which Weber called sublimation <ref type="bibr">(Weber, 1978, p. 25)</ref>.

text.text: Psychology describes the same passage in its own terms.
Multiple code theory describes a referential process that links subsymbolic bodily experience with symbolic and verbal codes (Bucci, 1997).
text.formatted: Multiple code theory describes a referential process that links subsymbolic bodily experience with symbolic and verbal codes <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Bucci, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: Alexithymia research treats weakness in this link as a disorder of affect regulation (Taylor et al., 1997).
text.formatted: Alexithymia research treats weakness in this link as a disorder of affect regulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Taylor et al., 1997)</ref>.

text.text: Constructionist work argues that language helps to make up both the experience and the perception of emotion (Lindquist et al., 2015).

text.text: Etzrodt's pair of opposites supplies the two failures.
He defines Durkheimian anomie as a person's inability to find and realize meaning in life.
Its cause is a lack of integration and regulation, or too much freedom (Etzrodt, 2024, p. 660).
text.formatted: Its cause is a lack of integration and regulation, or too much freedom <ref type="bibr">(Etzrodt, 2024, p. 660)</ref>.

text.text: He defines Marxist alienation, in general terms, as a state of being trapped by one's own creations, which prevents a person from developing freely (Etzrodt, 2024, pp. 659-660).
text.formatted: He defines Marxist alienation, in general terms, as a state of being trapped by one's own creations, which prevents a person from developing freely <ref type="bibr">(Etzrodt, 2024, pp. 659-660)</ref>.

text.text: Anomie results from too much freedom and alienation from too little, so that anomie is "formless life" and alienation is "lifeless form" (Thom, 1984 , as cited in Etzrodt, 2024, p. 660).
text.formatted: Anomie results from too much freedom and alienation from too little, so that anomie is "formless life" and alienation is "lifeless form" <ref type="bibr">(Thom, 1984</ref> <ref type="bibr">, as cited in Etzrodt, 2024, p. 660)</ref>.

text.text: In anomie the problem is a lack of meaning, while in alienation it is a lack of life (Etzrodt, 2024, p. 660).
text.formatted: In anomie the problem is a lack of meaning, while in alienation it is a lack of life <ref type="bibr">(Etzrodt, 2024, p. 660)</ref>.

text.text: This review transposes the pair from the relation between person and society to the relation between affect and linguistic form.
The transposition is an ideal-typical construction.
It does not claim that narcissistic speakers are anomic or alienated in the sociological sense.
Freedom keeps a precise meaning in the transposition.
It refers to how tightly affect is bound to linguistic form, not to how inhibited a person's conduct is.
In anomic expression affect is bound too loosely and escapes form.
In alienated expression it is bound too tightly to one self-made form.
A speaker who is bold in conduct therefore still cannot express what that form excludes.
Anomic expression is affect that lacks form.
It is not regulated by naming, and a listener cannot take it up.
Alienated expression is form that admits only the affects that fit it.
It is a self-made instrument of speech that has come to govern the speaker, and the speaker cannot revise it.
Collaborative expression lies between the two, where affect has form and the form stays open.
The types classify expressions, not people.
A person can stand closer to one pole on average, and the same speaker can fail on either side at different moments.
Trait measures therefore predict where a speaker's expression usually falls, and momentary measures track the shifts.
Table 1 sets out the two types.

text.text: >Ideal type A: anomic expression
text.formatted: <head n="5." >Ideal type A: anomic expression</head>

text.text: The type concerns spontaneous expression, that is, what happens to affect in ordinary speech without instruction.
If affect does not reach a speakable form there, three consequences follow.
First, the speaker loses the regulation that naming provides.
Labeling affect diminished the response of the amygdala to negative emotional images (Lieberman et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Labeling affect diminished the response of the amygdala to negative emotional images <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Lieberman et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Affect labeling regulates emotion implicitly, even when it does not feel like regulation (Torre & Lieberman, 2018).
text.formatted: Affect labeling regulates emotion implicitly, even when it does not feel like regulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Torre & Lieberman, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Second, emotional experience stays undifferentiated.
People who draw finer distinctions among their emotions are less likely to turn to binge drinking, aggression, or self-injury when distressed (Kashdan et al., 2015).
text.formatted: People who draw finer distinctions among their emotions are less likely to turn to binge drinking, aggression, or self-injury when distressed <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Kashdan et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: In the developmental model of emotional awareness, the lowest levels register emotion as bodily sensation or action tendency rather than as a differentiated feeling (Lane & Schwartz, 1987).
text.formatted: In the developmental model of emotional awareness, the lowest levels register emotion as bodily sensation or action tendency rather than as a differentiated feeling <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Lane & Schwartz, 1987)</ref>.

text.text: Third, the affect still seeks release, and without a form it is released as action.
Weber's description of affectual action as an uncontrolled reaction at the edge of meaning fits this case (Weber, 1978, p. 25).
text.formatted: Weber's description of affectual action as an uncontrolled reaction at the edge of meaning fits this case <ref type="bibr">(Weber, 1978, p. 25)</ref>.

text.text: The evidence near the vulnerable pole fits this derivation.
Narcissism correlates with difficulty identifying feelings (r = .14; k = 5), and samples that include vulnerable narcissism carry the positive correlation with alexithymia (Song et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Narcissism correlates with difficulty identifying feelings (r = .14; k = 5), and samples that include vulnerable narcissism carry the positive correlation with alexithymia <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Song et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The link between narcissism and emotion dysregulation is concentrated at the vulnerable pole (Tziliaskopoulos et al., 2027).
text.formatted: The link between narcissism and emotion dysregulation is concentrated at the vulnerable pole <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Tziliaskopoulos et al., 2027)</ref>.

text.text: In the same meta-analysis, the specific difficulties concerned accepting emotions, controlling impulses, and finding regulation strategies.
Vulnerable narcissism is also linked to habitual suppression (Walker et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Vulnerable narcissism is also linked to habitual suppression <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Walker et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: In an experimental study, people high in vulnerable narcissism reported suppressing emotion more often (Loeffler et al., 2020).
text.formatted: In an experimental study, people high in vulnerable narcissism reported suppressing emotion more often <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Loeffler et al., 2020</ref>).

text.text: Yet in the same study, narcissism was unrelated to the ability to regulate emotion on instruction.
This is the pattern the type specifies in advance: the failure lies in spontaneous expression, so instructed regulation is not the critical test.
The firmest support for the type comes from the dysregulation and suppression findings.
The alexithymia evidence shows the predicted signs, and Proposition 2 tests spontaneous naming directly.
Unnamed affect does not stay private.

Shame-proneness correlates with anger arousal, resentment, and a readiness to blame others when things go wrong (Tangney et al., 1992). Kohut (1972) described narcissistic rage as a reaction to injury of the self.

text.text: In a study of 405 adults, vulnerable narcissism predicted a tendency toward anger and hostility (Czarna et al., 2021).
text.formatted: In a study of 405 adults, vulnerable narcissism predicted a tendency toward anger and hostility <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Czarna et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Neuroticism accounted for much of this link, and poor strategic management of emotion contributed to hostility (Czarna et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Neuroticism accounted for much of this link, and poor strategic management of emotion contributed to hostility <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Czarna et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Anomic expression supplies a mechanism that connects these findings.
An injury that cannot be named as shame cannot be offered to a listener as a feeling.
It is voiced instead as an accusation or held back as withdrawal.
The listener then meets blame or silence and has no affect to respond to.
A simpler rival explains the vulnerable pole by neuroticism alone.
In dominance analyses across four samples, neuroticism accounted for 65% of the variance in vulnerable narcissism that the five-factor domains predicted (Miller et al., 2018).
text.formatted: In dominance analyses across four samples, neuroticism accounted for 65% of the variance in vulnerable narcissism that the five-factor domains predicted <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Miller et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: The variance not shared with neuroticism was specific to disagreeable traits such as distrustfulness and grandiosity (Miller et al., 2018).
text.formatted: The variance not shared with neuroticism was specific to disagreeable traits such as distrustfulness and grandiosity <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Miller et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: The ideal-type method turns this rival into a test.
Autism research offers a precedent.
The alexithymia hypothesis holds that emotional difficulties seen in autism stem from co-occurring alexithymia rather than from autism itself (Bird & Cook, 2013).
text.formatted: The alexithymia hypothesis holds that emotional difficulties seen in autism stem from co-occurring alexithymia rather than from autism itself <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bird & Cook, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Anomic expression is defined at the interface of affect and form.
It therefore predicts that failures of affect naming carry part of the link between vulnerable narcissism and anger, even when neuroticism is held constant (Proposition 3).
The disagreeable remainder is also where the type meets its opposite (Section 7).
>Ideal type B: alienated expression
text.formatted: <head n="6." >Ideal type B: alienated expression</head>

text.text: In general terms, alienation is a process in which people create things to make life easier and then find their lives dominated by those creations (Etzrodt, 2024, p. 659).
text.formatted: In general terms, alienation is a process in which people create things to make life easier and then find their lives dominated by those creations <ref type="bibr">(Etzrodt, 2024, p. 659)</ref>.

text.text: In expression, the created thing is the speaker's self-presentation.
Grandiose narcissism involves a moment-tomoment pursuit of social status (Grapsas et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Grandiose narcissism involves a moment-tomoment pursuit of social status <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Grapsas et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: In the admiration and rivalry model, a grandiose self is pursued through two pathways (Back et al., 2013).
text.formatted: In the admiration and rivalry model, a grandiose self is pursued through two pathways <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Back et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: The admiration pathway runs through dominant and expressive behavior that others read as assertive (Leckelt et al., 2015).
text.formatted: The admiration pathway runs through dominant and expressive behavior that others read as assertive <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Leckelt et al., 2015)</ref>.

text.text: A practiced self-presentation serves that pursuit.
Once established, it becomes the form through which each utterance must pass.
Three consequences follow.
Because the form is rehearsed, it is fluent.
Because the form has no place for feelings that do not fit it, such as doubt or shame, it is thin in those affects.

And because revising it would mean revising the self it presents, it is closed. Etzrodt (2024, p. 668) argues that Weber's iron cage is better explained by an extended concept of alienation than by disenchantment.
text.formatted: And because revising it would mean revising the self it presents, it is closed. <ref type="bibr">Etzrodt (2024, p. 668)</ref> argues that Weber's iron cage is better explained by an extended concept of alienation than by disenchantment.

text.text: Alienated expression is a small-scale version of that cage: a purposive instrument of speech that hardens into habit and then governs the speaker.
Schutz's analysis of habitual knowledge describes how such routines guide conduct without a fresh choice in each situation (Schutz & Luckmann, 1973).
text.formatted: Schutz's analysis of habitual knowledge describes how such routines guide conduct without a fresh choice in each situation <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Schutz & Luckmann, 1973)</ref>.

text.text: The fluency shows where a rehearsed form pays most: in brief, monologic, first encounters.
People high in narcissism are popular at zero acquaintance, and observable verbal and nonverbal behavior helps explain their appeal (Back et al., 2010).
text.formatted: People high in narcissism are popular at zero acquaintance, and observable verbal and nonverbal behavior helps explain their appeal <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Back et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Their pitches are judged creative partly because of their enthusiasm, although blind coders find their products no more creative than those of others (Goncalo et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Their pitches are judged creative partly because of their enthusiasm, although blind coders find their products no more creative than those of others <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Goncalo et al., 2010)</ref>.

Essays that must build an argument on the page are rated as relatively unpersuasive (Foster et al., 2025, Studies 2A to 2C).

Across 15 samples, grandiose narcissism correlated negatively with anxiety words and tentative words (Holtzman et al., 2019).

It was related to low affective empathy more strongly on behavioral measures (r = -.251) than on self-report (r = -.145; Urbonaviciute & Hepper, 2020).

People high in grandiose narcissism can thus infer what a listener thinks without sharing what the listener feels.

text.text: The type draws a distinction that a deficit account cannot draw.
Alienation, as defined above, concerns freedom rather than ability.

A systematic review reaches a compatible conclusion: the socialcognitive profile of narcissism may reflect motivation, or the self-serving use of intact skills, rather than deficit (Eddy, 2021).

text.text: The type also separates itself from a strategic-choice reading.
>Where the types meet
text.formatted: <head n="7." >Where the types meet</head>

text.text: The two types fail collaboration from opposite sides.
Anomic expression gives the listener no affect to take up, and alienated expression gives the listener no opening to change anything.
Both failures draw on antagonism.
The narcissism spectrum model places entitled self-importance at the core that grandiose and vulnerable narcissism share (Krizan & Herlache, 2018).
text.formatted: The narcissism spectrum model places entitled self-importance at the core that grandiose and vulnerable narcissism share <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Krizan & Herlache, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Self-centered antagonism is one of the three factors of narcissism (Crowe et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Self-centered antagonism is one of the three factors of narcissism <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Crowe et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: The variance in vulnerable narcissism that neuroticism does not explain is disagreeable (Miller et al., 2018).
text.formatted: The variance in vulnerable narcissism that neuroticism does not explain is disagreeable <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Miller et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Rivalry, the antagonistic side of grandiose narcissism, drives both the refusal to apologize and the decline in popularity (Leckelt et al., 2015; Leunissen et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Rivalry, the antagonistic side of grandiose narcissism, drives both the refusal to apologize and the decline in popularity <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Leckelt et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Leunissen et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Antagonism therefore explains why both poles fail at repair, and the types explain why they fail differently.
The types also fail on the same kind of affect.
At the grandiose pole the form still carries feeling.
Speakers high in narcissism pitch their ideas with enthusiasm (Goncalo et al., 2010), and their texts contain more swear words alongside fewer anxiety and tentative words (Holtzman et al., 2019).

text.text: The form is lifeless in a narrower sense.
It leaves out affect that would weaken the self it presents, such as doubt or the fear of falling short.
Neuroscience suggests that this affect is present but unreported.
Grandiose narcissism goes with heightened vigilance and stress responses after ego threat, and self-reports seldom show these responses (Jauk & Kanske, 2021).
text.formatted: Grandiose narcissism goes with heightened vigilance and stress responses after ego threat, and self-reports seldom show these responses <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Jauk & Kanske, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: The type names shame as the prototype of the excluded affect.
A systematic review of 27 studies finds the two poles split on shame in the directions the types imply (Kesman et al., 2026).
text.formatted: A systematic review of 27 studies finds the two poles split on shame in the directions the types imply <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Kesman et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: In its nonclinical samples, vulnerable narcissism related positively to shame, with moderate to strong effects.
Grandiose narcissism measured with the Narcissistic Personality Inventory related slightly negatively.
Links were more variable for pathological grandiosity, which the review reads as a more reactive form.
That reactivity fits the movement described in Section 7.3.
In its clinical studies, narcissistic personality disorder went with low shame-proneness but high shame aversion and elevated implicit shame.
The review concludes that it is shame, not guilt, that differentiates the two poles (Kesman et al., 2026).
text.formatted: The review concludes that it is shame, not guilt, that differentiates the two poles <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Kesman et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Shame is therefore the affect that the two poles share and handle in opposite ways.
In anomic expression it floods the speaker without reaching words.
In alienated expression it is kept out of the form, which stays fluent because it never has to carry shame.
Propositions 2 and 4 test the naming side of this claim.
Both predict that naming failures concentrate on shame and related self-conscious emotions.
A general deficit in identifying feelings, as in alexithymia, predicts no such concentration.
The types also account for movement between the poles.
Dispositionally grandiose people report vulnerable as well as grandiose states, and entitlement is central to these momentary processes (Edershile & Wright, 2021).
text.formatted: Dispositionally grandiose people report vulnerable as well as grandiose states, and entitlement is central to these momentary processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Edershile & Wright, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Under the framework, such a shift is a movement of the same speaker from alienated to anomic expression.
It should be most likely when shame breaks through the self-presentation that holds the form together.
An experiment supports this sequence.
Young adolescents high in narcissism became more aggressive than their peers only once they had been shamed (Thomaes et al., 2008).
text.formatted: Young adolescents high in narcissism became more aggressive than their peers only once they had been shamed <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Thomaes et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: The effect was strongest when narcissism came with high self-esteem, a combination close to the grandiose pole.
The aggression is the anomic outcome that Section 5.3 describes.

Jauk and Kanske's (2021) review of 34 neuroscience studies also links interpersonal functioning in narcissism to deficits in social-affective processing, with altered activity in the salience network.
These findings converge on an interface between affect and social processing, as the types expect.
If the expressive difficulty in narcissism were a structural language deficit, childhood language disorder should predict narcissistic pathology in proportion to its severity.
The evidence shows risk without that proportion.
In the Danish cohort, personality disorder diagnoses were more than twice as common among people diagnosed with developmental language disorder in childhood (Mouridsen & Hauschild, 2009).
text.formatted: In the Danish cohort, personality disorder diagnoses were more than twice as common among people diagnosed with developmental language disorder in childhood <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Mouridsen & Hauschild, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Yet sex, IQ, the presence of receptive impairment, and the degree of expressive and receptive impairment did not predict a diagnosis (Mouridsen & Hauschild, 2009).
text.formatted: Yet sex, IQ, the presence of receptive impairment, and the degree of expressive and receptive impairment did not predict a diagnosis <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Mouridsen & Hauschild, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: The same cohort shows that a dose-response relation can appear: the degree of expressive language disorder was associated with schizophrenia-spectrum diagnoses (Mouridsen & Hauschild, 2008).

text.text: The absence of such a relation for personality disorder is therefore informative.
It suggests that the path runs through the experiences that language disorder brings rather than through language structure itself.
Two such experiences fit the framework: weaker emotion regulation and social anxiety.
Children with language impairment receive lower teacher ratings of emotion regulation than their peers (Fujiki et al., 2002).
text.formatted: Children with language impairment receive lower teacher ratings of emotion regulation than their peers <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Fujiki et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: The finding suggests a route toward the anomic type, which Proposition 7 tests.
Early language impairment also predicts anxiety disorders in young adulthood, most of them social phobia (Beitchman et al., 2001).
text.formatted: Early language impairment also predicts anxiety disorders in young adulthood, most of them social phobia <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Beitchman et al., 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Childhood ability shows no single direction either.
In a population sample of 4,713 nine-yearolds, narcissistic traits went with higher verbal and nonverbal ability (Fontaine et al., 2008).
text.formatted: In a population sample of 4,713 nine-yearolds, narcissistic traits went with higher verbal and nonverbal ability <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Fontaine et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: The association held after conduct problems and hyperactivity were taken into account.
Among 361 adolescents from samples with different levels of risk for antisocial behavior, narcissism was unrelated to verbal ability and related to lower nonverbal ability (Allen et al., 2013).

text.text: Low language ability is therefore not a uniform risk direction for narcissism.
Developmental language disorder is best treated as a distal marker of vulnerability whose effects pass through emotion regulation and social experience.
Under the framework, it raises the likelihood of anomic expression without causing it.
Each proposition below follows from the types and is paired with the observation that would refute it.
Propositions 1 to 4 test the defining features of the types.
Propositions 5 to 7 test consequences of those features for modality, choice, and development.
Table 2 lists measures suited to each test.

text.text: Narcissism at either pole relates more strongly to indicators of the affect-form relation than to structural language indicators.
The first include spontaneous affect naming, emotional granularity, and repair and apology in conversation; the second include vocabulary, grammar, and sentence complexity.
Because pragmatic measures depend partly on structural language (Norbury, 2014), the test holds structural language constant.
text.formatted: Because pragmatic measures depend partly on structural language <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Norbury, 2014)</ref>, the test holds structural language constant.

text.text: Refutation: structural indicators relate to narcissism as strongly as affect-form indicators do, or the affectform link disappears once structural language is controlled.
Proposition 2 (anomic expression in performance).
Vulnerable narcissism predicts weaker spontaneous affect naming on performance and observer measures, beyond higher self-reported difficulty identifying feelings.
The deficit is largest for shame and other self-conscious emotions.
The test therefore needs naming tasks that include shame-eliciting scenes, scored apart from scenes that elicit basic emotions.
Refutation: performance-based emotional awareness and observer-rated alexithymia show no deficit at the vulnerable pole.
The proposition also fails if the deficit is equal across emotion categories, in which case general alexithymia suffices.
Proposition 3 (the anomic path beyond neuroticism).
Weak affect naming carries part of the association between vulnerable narcissism and anger or blame in conflict talk.
This indirect path remains when neuroticism is held constant.
Refutation: affect naming carries none of the association, or the path disappears once neuroticism is controlled.
In that case the vulnerable pole reduces to neuroticism.
The grandiose advantage on selfreported alexithymia and trait emotional intelligence shrinks or reverses on performance and observer measures.
The gap is also larger for affective than for cognitive skills.
This second prediction separates the type from general self-enhancement, which predicts overstatement of both.
Within affect, the gap is largest for shame and other self-threatening emotions.
Refutation: the advantage holds equally on performance-based emotional awareness, ability emotional intelligence, and observer ratings.
The proposition also fails if the gap is no larger for affective than for cognitive skills, or no larger for self-threatening than for other emotions.
Proposition 5 (modality, dialogue, and time).
Within the same persons, grandiose narcissism predicts higher rated persuasiveness in spoken monologue at first acquaintance.
The advantage shrinks or reverses in writing, in dialogic tasks, and over repeated contact.
The minimal design has the same speakers give a speech and write an essay in counterbalanced order, rated by blind raters.
Refutation: the advantage appears as strongly in written or dialogic tasks, or the spoken advantage fails to appear within persons.
Incentives that reward collaboration do not by themselves change the self-promoting form of grandiose speakers, whereas perspective-taking instruction does.
The comparison is fixed in advance: the instruction effect should exceed the incentive effect.
Manipulation checks confirm that participants registered the incentive and adopted the perspective.
Refutation: the incentive effect equals or exceeds the instruction effect, which would favor a strategic-choice reading over the alienation type.
A history of developmental language disorder relates to later personality pathology through emotion regulation and peer experience rather than through childhood language severity.
It also relates more closely to anomic than to alienated features.
The test controls for executive function and family socioeconomic status, which could drive both language and later outcomes.
Refutation: childhood severity predicts later narcissistic features after these paths are taken into account, or a history of language disorder relates equally to both types.

text.text: Three rival accounts explain parts of the evidence.
A structural-deficit account treats the difficulty as low language ability.
A trait-only account derives it from the three factors of narcissism (Crowe et al., 2019; Miller et al., 2018).
text.formatted: A trait-only account derives it from the three factors of narcissism <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Crowe et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Miller et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: On this account, neuroticism makes people poor at naming feelings and prone to anger, agentic extraversion makes them fluent and selfassured, and antagonism makes them uncooperative.
A strategic-choice account treats grandiose speech as a rational choice of tactics (Hart et al., 2017).
text.formatted: A strategic-choice account treats grandiose speech as a rational choice of tactics <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Hart et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Table 3 sets out where the four accounts diverge.

text.text: The trait-only account is the strongest rival, and five predictions separate it from the types.
First, the types predict a self-report bias that runs in opposite directions at the two poles.
At the grandiose pole, they also predict a larger bias for affective than for cognitive skill, an asymmetry a trait account has no reason to expect.
The empathy meta-analysis shows it (Urbonaviciute & Hepper, 2020).
text.formatted: The empathy meta-analysis shows it <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Urbonaviciute & Hepper, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: At the grandiose pole, self-reports understate the affective deficit that behavioral measures reveal, while behavioral measures show cognitive empathy intact.
Second, the types predict that affect naming carries part of the vulnerable link to anger after neuroticism is controlled (Proposition 3).
The trait account expects neuroticism to absorb it.
Third, the types predict that instruction changes grandiose speech more than incentive does (Proposition 6), a contrast on which the trait account is silent.
Fourth, the types predict a shift from alienated to anomic expression when the self-presentation is threatened.

A stable trait profile does not entail that within-person shift, which momentary, experimental, and neuroscientific evidence makes plausible (Edershile & Wright, 2021; Jauk & Kanske, 2021; Thomaes et al., 2008).

text.text: Fifth, the types predict that naming failures concentrate on shame and related self-conscious emotions (Propositions 2 and 4).
A trait account, like a general alexithymia account, predicts difficulty across emotions.
Existing data already count against the other two rivals.

text.text: The framework solves six problems that the separate literatures leave open.
The first is a classification problem.
Asking whether narcissism involves expressive language disorder pairs a structural diagnosis with a problem of affect and form.
Relocating the difficulty explains why direct searches find nothing, and why a speaker high in narcissism can be fluent and inarticulate at once.
The second is an aggregation problem.
A near-zero correlation between narcissism and alexithymia (Song et al., 2026) is what two opposite failures produce when they are pooled.
text.formatted: A near-zero correlation between narcissism and alexithymia <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Song et al., 2026)</ref> is what two opposite failures produce when they are pooled.

text.text: The types also predict the signs that the moderator analyses found.
The third is a measurement problem.
The gap between grandiose self-reports and performance (Michels & Schulze, 2021) becomes a predicted property of alienated expression, which tells researchers where self-report will mislead.
text.formatted: The gap between grandiose self-reports and performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Michels & Schulze, 2021)</ref> becomes a predicted property of alienated expression, which tells researchers where self-report will mislead.

text.text: The fourth is a specificity problem.
Speakers at the grandiose pole pitch with enthusiasm and swear more, yet use fewer anxiety and tentative words (Goncalo et al., 2010; Holtzman et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Speakers at the grandiose pole pitch with enthusiasm and swear more, yet use fewer anxiety and tentative words <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Goncalo et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Holtzman et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: The types expect this selectivity, because the alienated form keeps out the affects that threaten the self.
Shame is the prototype of those affects, and it is also the affect that the anomic speaker cannot name.
Naming failures should therefore concentrate on shame and related self-conscious emotions rather than spread across all emotions.
The fifth is a developmental anomaly.
Developmental language disorder raises the risk of personality disorder without a dose-response relation to severity (Mouridsen & Hauschild, 2009).
text.formatted: Developmental language disorder raises the risk of personality disorder without a dose-response relation to severity <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Mouridsen & Hauschild, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: The framework expects this, because the relevant failure lies in the relation between affect and form rather than in structural language.
The sixth is a testing problem.
Seven propositions, each with a refutation condition, give the field a way to decide between the types and their rivals.
For assessment, the framework recommends pairing every self-report of emotional skill with a performance or observer measure, and coding conversation for repair, apology, and expressed uncertainty.
Affect naming should be scored separately for self-conscious emotions, such as shame, and for basic emotions.
A total score would hide a failure concentrated on shame.
For intervention, the framework separates two needs.
At the anomic pole, the task is to give affect, and shame above all, a form.
Work that builds affect labeling and emotion differentiation targets that failure directly (Kashdan et al., 2015; Torre & Lieberman, 2018).
text.formatted: Work that builds affect labeling and emotion differentiation targets that failure directly <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Kashdan et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Torre & Lieberman, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: At the alienated pole, vocabulary is not the problem.
The task is to open the form to the affects it excludes.
Perspective-taking instructions raise empathy in people high in narcissism, which shows that this is possible (Hepper et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Perspective-taking instructions raise empathy in people high in narcissism, which shows that this is possible <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Hepper et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: A single protocol for both poles would leave one of the two failures untreated.
The review also extends Etzrodt's reading of anomie and alienation.
Etzrodt (2024) uses these concepts to interpret Weber's rationalization processes in economic, political, and religious life.
Defined at the level of a single speaker, the same pair organizes a two-faced construct in personality psychology as two opposite failures of one relation.
The result is a template for other constructs with a grandiose and a vulnerable face.
Instead of averaging the faces, researchers can define the relation that both disturb and derive each face as an ideal type with its own refutation conditions.
The framework makes no diagnostic claim, and its types classify expressions rather than persons.
The difficulties it describes sit at the interface of affect and pragmatic form.
They are not equivalent to language disorder or social (pragmatic) communication disorder in DSM-5-TR, or to their ICD counterparts.
This scope keeps the framework from pathologizing pragmatic difference.
In the evidence reviewed here, narcissism leaves language ability intact but disturbs the relation between affect and form, in two opposite ways.
At one pole, affect finds no form and returns as anger or silence.
At the other, form keeps out the affects that would threaten it and stays fixed after it stops working.
Shame is the affect at stake in both.
Weber's ideal types, extended by falsification as Etzrodt proposes, make the two failures precise enough to test.
Etzrodt's pair of anomie and alienation names them: formless affect and lifeless fluency.
The research question therefore becomes whether the affect of people high in narcissism reaches a form that another person can take up and change.
